opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, SGLang has become much more central to my plans than I expected when we started it.

In the beginning, it was really a research project. We were looking at how people were actually using large language models: not just single prompts, but complex programs with multiple calls, branching, structured outputs, agents, and so on. We saw a lot of waste in how these workloads were being served. The same prefixes were being recomputed again and again, and the frontend and backend weren't designed together. So the original idea was fairly academic: if we co-design the language for expressing these LLM programs with the runtime that executes them, how much efficiency can we get? Things like RadixAttention for automatic KV cache reuse came out of that thinking.

What changed is that people started using it for real. Once the community picked it up, and companies began running it in production for serving and for reinforcement learning rollouts, it stopped being just a paper artifact. It became infrastructure. That shifted my priorities quite a bit. I had to think less like a researcher optimizing for one novel idea and more like someone responsible for a system that a lot of people depend on: reliability, supporting new models on day one, working across different hardware, and building a healthy open-source community with many contributors.

So now I see SGLang as a foundation for a lot of what I want to do. I've always cared about making AI systems efficient and accessible. Inference cost is one of the biggest barriers to deploying these models widely, and if we can make serving faster and cheaper in the open, it benefits everyone, from big labs to students with a single GPU. SGLang is the vehicle for that. It also keeps me close to the frontier, because every time a new model architecture or a new usage pattern appears, we see it immediately in the issues and pull requests.

So in short: it started as a research question, it grew into a community, and now it's really the center of how I think about my work going forward.

r001.rationale: The response says SGLang became more central than expected and is now central to her future work, but it does not clearly say it remained central throughout the period since she started it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, SGLang started as something pretty practical. When we were building complex LLM programs at Berkeley, we kept running into the same friction: you'd write these multi-step prompts with branching, parallel calls, constrained decoding, and the frontend abstractions were clunky while the backend was wasting a huge amount of compute re-processing shared prefixes. So the first idea was really two things together, a structured language for programming LLMs, and a runtime underneath, with RadixAttention for KV cache reuse, that could actually make those programs fast.

What I didn't fully anticipate is how much the backend would take over. People wanted a fast, open inference engine more than they wanted a new DSL, so the serving side became the center of gravity. And that changed my plans a lot. It stopped being a research artifact and became something companies were deploying in production, which meant we had to care about things like stability, multi-node serving, quantization, and supporting every new model architecture the week it comes out.

For me personally, it's become the thing I organize my work around. It's the bridge between the research I care about, like scheduling and cache management and speculative decoding, and real-world impact, because any improvement we land gets used almost immediately by a lot of people. It's also taught me that building an open-source community is its own kind of research problem. So the plan now is less "finish this project" and more "keep SGLang as the place where the best serving ideas get implemented first."

r001.rationale: The response says SGLang is now what she organizes her work around, but describes its role as changing over time. It does not clearly state that it remained central to her plans from the start.

astra-6.text: For me, SGLang has been a way to bring our research on efficient inference into a system people can actually use. From the beginning, I wanted to work on both sides: exploring new ideas and understanding what matters when you deploy them. SGLang connects those two. You build something, people use it, and their feedback helps you figure out which problems to tackle next.

r001.rationale: She describes SGLang as the way she has pursued both research and deployment from the beginning, and says it connects those aims—communicating its ongoing central role in her plans.

sol-6.1.text: SGLang has been a way for me to bring research ideas into a system that people can actually use. With language models, an algorithm can look promising in an experiment, but making it efficient and useful in practice brings a different set of challenges. Working on SGLang creates that feedback loop: research informs the system, and real workloads reveal the next research questions. So I see it as both a research platform and an open-source project that we want to keep making more useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes SGLang as a research platform and ongoing open-source project, but does not state that it has remained central to Ying Sheng’s plans since she started it.
